11–12 October 2026 · woby 0.29.0 · revision e856e03d778d520a7a60ba0a30b7651b8f639c16

BearTrap OBJ: where the load time goes

12 October: hardware counters, kernel controls and native viewer tests

The new tools provide real AMD core-counter samples and two independent CPU profiles. Native tests identify useful changes in memory capacity, attribute access, bounds reduction and upload pacing.

  • Reserve growth: 624.4 MiB less retained mesh capacity, with identical geometry.
  • UV pointer capture: 8.4% less corner-mapping time; 1.8% less CPU-ready time in four native paired rounds.
  • Bounds: direct validated access, register reductions and independent workers are larger opportunities than removing one index level.
  • Hidden upload: shorter inactive-frame pacing cuts the native load endpoint from 47.13 s to 37.55 s, with almost unchanged CPU preparation.
  • GPU use: settled hidden rendering reaches 61.7 frames/s and 99% device-wide busy time under the research pacing. Its higher GPU clock and power are part of that result.

The 11 October baseline below is a separate batch. It took 43.31 s for SSE2 CPU preparation; current native baselines are about 35 s. The production source is unchanged. The difference between days is not assigned to an optimization. Use the same-batch paired results for claims about changes. CPU frequency and temperature were not recorded per stage.

Hardware measurements by phase

AMD uProf 5.3.521.0 collected core PMCs on the Ryzen 7 5800H. Counter sets fit the six reported core counters: cycles + retired instructions plus branch/DTLB, demand-fill/dispatch, or FP events. The FP event uses a paired merge counter. Counts below are sample counts multiplied by each event's period. User mode is enabled; OS events are excluded.

Phase markers have absolute QPC timestamps and are aligned to native collection metadata; those offsets are about 16–21 ms. The short calibration below exposes a further approximately 16 ms residual difference in the database time origin. Each phase includes a +16 ms sensitivity check. Phase selection uses start-inclusive, end-exclusive windows. Short phases below 100 ms are omitted from counter ratios. Parent phases overlap their children and must not be added to them.

Corner mapping retires about 197.6 instructions per corner in the SSE2 branch capture. Its estimated branch miss rate is 0.556%, or 1.01 misses per 1,000 instructions. Branch prediction is effective here. The secondary seam hash also covers only 0.58% of corners. These findings focus attention on repeated attribute access and instruction count.

Group original bounds has an IPC estimate of 2.49 with SSE2 and 4.27 with AVX2. Retired instruction estimates fall from 27.26 B to 19.29 B. This supports a compiler/code-path explanation for the large bounds gain. It does not show that 256-bit arithmetic processes eight vertices at a time.

The FP event was checked with a known SSE2 loop: 536,870,912 expected FP operations and 535,000,000 estimated operations, an error of -0.35%. AMD's event requires a merged counter; uProf handles that configuration. This calibration supports the FP estimates but does not turn sampled data into exact totals.

Local-DRAM/IO demand-fill counts exclude prefetch fills, stores and other traffic. Multiplying them by 64 bytes does not measure physical DRAM bandwidth. DTLB miss counts do not give page-walk duration. FP counts include arithmetic in unused vector lanes; they are not a count of useful geometry operations. Comparisons and blend instructions are not included as FP arithmetic. No zero counter is interpreted as proof that the event never occurred. The raw event definitions, sample counts and time ranges are preserved.

Validate the hotspot in production code

The production UV getter accounts for 6.23% of sampled user cycles across the complete load. Its 23-byte body follows four dependent pointers before reading and converting the double UV value. The probe attributes about 49% of corner-mapping cycle samples to the same getter. The production capture confirms that the code path is real; native paired runs measure the useful gain from changing it.

2271e0: mov rax, qword ptr [rcx]
2271e3: mov rcx, qword ptr [rax]
2271e6: mov rax, qword ptr [rcx + 8]
2271ea: mov rcx, qword ptr [rax]
2271ed: movsd xmm0, qword ptr [rcx + rdx*8]
2271f2: cvtpd2ps xmm0, xmm0
2271f6: ret

These loads usually hit small metadata in cache. Their serial dependencies can still cost time. Capturing the immutable UV data pointer removes repeated metadata loads. The remaining corner work and memory access limit the total gain. Event-based sampling can skid, so the sample share is not a direct prediction of removable wall time.

VTune's independent user-mode capture also identifies this getter: 4.499 s of sampled CPU time, after ParseFace at 9.047 s and fast_float numeric conversion at 7.485 s. VTune reports 96.566 s of aggregate CPU time over 43.364 s, with 4.624 s classified as spin. That capture includes the probe's separate geometry fingerprint validation. It therefore measures more than loading alone; its spin label does not establish a kernel wait cause.

The VTune main thread accounts for 37.055 s of sampled CPU time, including fingerprint validation. Sixteen worker threads each account for 3.399–4.269 s. Their work is reasonably balanced by aggregate CPU time. These are different threads and a different process from the NVTX capture; thread IDs must not be joined across the captures.

Native experiments: gains and a negative result

Research changeCPU-ready median sMedian time reductionPaired round time reductions
Reserve 2% more source IDs35.532 → 35.032+1.40%-0.33 to +2.14%
Precompute valid-UV flags35.473 → 36.082-1.72%-2.60 to -1.66%
Capture the UV data pointer35.255 → 34.634+1.76%+0.63 to +3.41%

The 2% reserve saves 654,750,324 bytes (624.4 MiB) of retained mesh capacity. Its timing gain is small and varies by round. The memory reduction is the stronger result. This is a model-specific estimate: models with more UV/normal seams can need a different reserve strategy.

The valid-UV cache adds one byte per UV, about 38.4 MB, and a 0.249 s prepass. All four paired import times are slower. The pointer experiment changes only the getter capture; the paired chart shows its actual effect. A hotspot in sampled data does not guarantee a useful wall-time change.

All three experiments produce identical complete geometry and normal fingerprints on this model. Small fixture tests also cover UV seams, unused invalid UV values, and values that overflow float conversion. These are research targets. The production loader remains unchanged.

A separate hardware capture supports the pointer result. Estimated corner-loop retired instructions fall from 44.914 B to 43.343 B; cycles fall from 22.518 B to 20.496 B. IPC rises from 1.99 to 2.11. DRAM/IO demand-fill estimates stay close: 54.800 M versus 54.375 M. This supports less instruction/dependency work as the reason for the gain. Separate profiler captures are diagnostic; the native paired runs establish wall time.

Isolate value selection and 128-bit SIMD

The compiler's SSE2 min/max uses floating comparison, an integer conditional move of a pointer, and a dependent value load. AVX code uses vcmpltsd and vblendvpd. The latter operates on XMM registers here. This is a value-selection change; it does not require 256-bit vectors or AVX2 integer instructions.

SSE2 compiler sequence for one minimum:
movsd   xmm0, [box]
comisd  xmm0, [point]
mov     rax, box_address
cmova   rax, point_address
mov     rax, [rax]             ; chosen value after pointer selection
mov     [box], rax

AVX compiler sequence:
vmovsd    xmm2, [box]
vmovsd    xmm1, [point]
vcmpltsd  xmm0, xmm1, xmm2
vblendvpd xmm0, xmm2, xmm1, xmm0
vmovsd   [box], xmm0

The explicit SSE2 mask kernel uses compare, AND, AND-NOT and OR to select values. SSE4.1 replaces that selection with a blend. Both keep reduction values in registers across iterations. This test separates register-based reduction from the compiler ISA switch. It is a specialized kernel for validated finite OBJ coordinates; general mesh access and empty/partial group handling still need the production contract.

Read/decode concurrency and serial work

All 16 read/decode workers overlap. Their completion times are uneven. The subsequent corner map, group bounds and most point preparation execute serially. This timeline was captured with NVTX only; CPU sampling and context switches were disabled because those Nsight modes require more access in this session. The stage CPU counters and uProf samples provide separate evidence of CPU use.

Observed instruction forms and calibration

AVX2 mainly replaces SSE encodings with VEX scalar or 128-bit instructions in these kernels. Wide AVX is present in memory routines and some generated code. The mapping and sorting work remains dominated by integer operations and control flow. Intel SDE is still absent, so exact per-phase dynamic SSE/AVX instruction counts remain open.

The loop executes 402,653,184 x86 instructions. Its 403 retired-event samples estimate 403,000,000 instructions, +0.09% from the known count. Yet 98.3% of sampled loop IPs point at FP arithmetic, compared with the known 66.7% dynamic fraction. Sampling period effects and skid can strongly bias opcode-location shares. This is why the ISA plots describe observed locations rather than exact instruction utilization.

The control's loop sample activity spans about 32–484 ms in the native database. The metadata/QPC phase window predicts about 16.5–469.2 ms. That exposes an approximately 16 ms residual origin difference. Whole-loop calibration counts do not require phase-window selection. The phase tables include a +16 ms sensitivity check; long-phase conclusions are more robust than subsecond ratios.

The production hidden viewer permits at most 16 MiB per 50 ms frame. This payload needs at least 169 frames, or about 8.40 s between first and last frame even if the copy cost were negligible. The native research viewer logs 170 upload frames over 1.487 s. Their payload sum is 2,823,231,768 bytes. Pacing and the per-frame byte cap are part of observed upload latency.

Summed step time includes staging copies, queue operations and waits. It is not PCIe transfer time. The elapsed frame interval includes pacing and other work. Neither measure alone establishes PCIe bandwidth or copy-engine occupancy. A Vulkan GPU timeline is still required to separate these costs.

Both recordings wait 25 s after screenshot capture before measuring eight seconds of ordinary frames. This reduces overlap with the annotation worker; the process CPU trace can be checked for residual work. The 1 ms experiment measures a hidden-window workload with different pacing. It is not a visible-window FPS result. NVML power, clock and temperature are coarse device samples. Its constant 100% memory-utilization field is excluded from bandwidth conclusions.

GPU busy before model upload covers the progress/UI workload and other applications. OBJ parsing and CPU mesh preparation remain CPU work. Device-wide GPU activity does not show that the parser runs on the GPU.

The faster GPU frame time includes a higher SM clock: about 1,875 MHz versus 1,575 MHz in the production hidden run. This is a workload/power-state correlation, not a geometry or shader optimization. The same camera, 1280×720 drawable, 805×687 model viewport and 4× MSAA remain in use. Each viewer has one native capture; these results do not establish a statistical FPS distribution across machines.

The settled viewer has 2.872 GiB of queried write-combined committed pages, with only 39.61 MiB marked Valid. This accounts for much of the gap between private commit and the working set. Their page protection, size distribution and load/remove lifetime are consistent with graphics mappings. That attribution is an inference; the page APIs do not provide the driver allocation owner or VRAM placement.

The largest cached private allocation has 1.819 GB committed and 1.229 GB of valid pages. These sizes match the vertex-capacity and populated-vertex sizes; the identity is inferred from size rather than an allocation stack. Thus reducing spare vector capacity reduces commit without necessarily saving the same amount of steady resident RAM. Native reserve tests separately show a lower import RSS peak.

The queried-page inventory excludes allocations below 1 MiB. Valid pages can include large pages or special mappings outside the ordinary working set, and the scan spans multiple kernel calls. Its total need not equal the later process RSS reading. The loaded scans take about 2.2–2.4 s, so these captures are memory controls and are not used for native timing comparisons.

The source retains the five mesh arrays, point-cloud arrays and later annotation arrays shown in the CPU memory diagram. GPU geometry uses device-local allocations; its Buffer struct holds an owner and size/stride fields. The upload queue keeps one fixed 16 MiB CPU-visible ring. It copies each source range immediately and reuses ring space after GPU completion. It does not retain a full CPU shadow of all GPU geometry. Three frame arenas also retain reusable pages, normally at least 4 MiB per used arena.

VirtualQueryEx classifies virtual page ranges. It does not identify the C++ object that allocated them, and its committed-page totals are not identical to the process private-commit counter. Copy-on-write pages keep their mapped/image type. This API alone does not establish page residency. The scan is read-only and not atomic; annotation and rendering can run during a checkpoint. Heap allocation stacks and driver allocation records are still required to assign every byte.

Scene history copies file metadata, not the mesh arrays. Model removal and creating a new empty scene are measured separately. The latter also resets runtime state; the intervening time permits delayed graphics cleanup. A later decrease cannot be assigned only to undo-history clearing. The final empty checkpoint tests release after more GPU retirement and worker time. Two load/remove captures do not establish long-term leak behavior.

Tool installation does not guarantee access to every source. This session is not elevated. Hyper-V is active, and uProf reports several sources unavailable; that inventory does not prove the cause of each unavailable source. Failed attempts and their messages are in the archive. No system profiling policy, virtualization setting or NVIDIA counter-access setting was changed.

The next most useful capture is an elevated ETW CPU/context-switch/I/O trace plus a Vulkan GPU timeline with counter access. That would distinguish runnable delay, allocation, file waits, staging copy, fence waits and GPU copy work. After access is available, use the same model, camera and native paired controls. Keep exact opcode counting in a separate SDE run.

Further loader candidates now have evidence: reuse complete-group bounds, add validated specialized reductions, parallelize independent bounds, and keep the UV pointer stable. Reserve growth should be bounded for models with many seams. Defer point preparation only after checking picking and marker behavior. Test cancellation and partial groups before promoting a research kernel. A binary cache or a different file format can avoid ASCII conversion on repeated loads, but needs its own versioning, invalidation, storage-size and cold-load tests.

11 October: first-pass timings and complete data flow

The largest costs are serial corner mapping and bounds preparation. The parser already uses most CPU threads. The AVX2 compiler experiment helps bounds work, with little change to parsing or mapping.

The current SSE2 probe takes 43.31 s to import the model and prepare CPU data for upload. The same six source units compiled with AVX2 take 37.57 s: 13.2% less time, or 1.15× throughput. These values are medians of three paired, rotating, fresh-process runs per build. The SSE2 range is 41.73–43.66 s; the AVX2 range is 37.53–38.17 s. GPU upload, rendering, and the validation hash are outside this CPU total. Three runs do not establish a confidence interval for small differences.

Data flow: what each step reads and creates

Follow the arrows from file text to pixels. Letter IDs identify the same buffers across diagrams. Horizontal arrows in each detailed map show inputs and outputs; dashed vertical arrows show execution order. In the overview, forks show data reuse and do not imply that the branches run in parallel. Only the annotation branch starts on a separate worker after scene publication.

The origin pass validates double source coordinates. The following pass subtracts the origin. This model uses a zero origin, but the current code still traverses and rewrites its position array. Triangulation mainly inspects already triangular faces. The mesh builder adopts the source coordinate buffer; it does not copy a second full XYZ buffer.

The final CPU mesh then needs per-group local and original-coordinate bounds. The group original-coordinate pass walks all 227,315,958 corners, while whole-mesh original bounds earlier walked render vertices. On this one-group model, that is repeated work over the same geometry. The group radius uses the bounding box; the whole-mesh radius uses vertex distances, so those radius values need distinct handling when bounds are reused.

Going from 8 to 16 workers improves parser time by 27.3%. The 16-worker setting is useful on this eight-core CPU. Thread affinity was not fixed, so this does not isolate SMT from scheduling effects. One worker uses the bounded chunk path; larger worker counts use persistent file ranges, so this comparison includes that internal path difference. At 16 workers there are 16 ranges and a reported 64 MiB text-storage bound. Parsed chunk data is approximately 4.55 GB and is separate from that text bound.

The read/decode interval overlaps file reads, conversion, chunk allocation, and ordered collection. Worker submit/wait times are summed across overlapping workers. They are not a separate wall-time stage and cannot be subtracted from total parser time to obtain disk latency.

The production unified parser opens a buffered, overlapped Windows handle. Each benchmark warms the file immediately before the process starts. These parser timings therefore measure cached loading. The read-native control bypasses the Windows file cache and uses aligned 256 KiB reads. It measures the input device separately; it is not a measurement of cold production parsing. No system cache was flushed. Cached and native read controls use synchronous reads in each worker, while the parser overlaps reads with decoding.

A separate 512 MiB copy test, with two initialized buffers and 16 copies per process, reaches 13.05 GB/s of payload copy throughput (at least 26.10 GB/s of read-plus-write traffic). This is a calibration for contiguous copies. Mesh gathers, validation, table updates and branches cannot be assigned that bandwidth.

Only 0.58% of corners enter the secondary seam hash lookup. First use and primary hits account for the rest. The diagnostic build adds counters, so its time is not used in the timing tables. Mapping is 15.05 million corners/s in the current SSE2 timing probe.

Mapping also validates UV values, checks source indices, gathers source coordinates, constructs vertices, records source IDs, and writes two index streams. The primary array occupies 144.5 MiB; key capacity is 650.4 MiB; hash buckets occupy 4.0 MiB. A faster hash function alone cannot remove most of this work.

The primary and key arrays each exceed the 16 MiB L3 cache. This makes access order and repeated coordinate gathers useful targets for investigation. It does not prove a measured cache-miss rate.

Median import peak working set is 9.241 GiB, approximately 14.5% of installed usable RAM. This excludes GPU allocation and the Windows input file cache. Retained mesh buffer capacity is 4.446 GiB; populated geometry arrays account for about 3.829 GiB. Capacity growth leaves about 0.618 GiB unused. Vertex, key and position-map capacities grow from a source-position estimate when UV seams add vertices.

CPU instructions: source, assembly and samples

StageInstruction evidence
Text and number decodeInteger loads, branches, shifts and multiplies; fast_float uses 64-bit SWAR for eligible eight-digit runs. Scalar SSE2 double operations remain in numeric conversion.
Corner mappingInteger index/table operations plus SSE moves and float conversion. The AVX2 build adds VEX forms and wider record moves; it does not become a wide parallel mapping kernel.
Normal generationScalar mulss, subss, sqrtss, divss and addss; a packed divps operation normalizes components. AVX2 uses the corresponding VEX forms, still mostly scalar arithmetic.
BoundsScalar FP comparisons and coordinate operations. AVX2 enables blend instructions and changes register/copy code. Much of the gain occurs in original-coordinate group bounds.
Point hierarchyInteger Morton coding and radix sorting; scalar FP normalization and coordinate gathers. No explicit AVX2 sorting kernel.
Runtime memory routinesRead the sampled-instruction results below. The Windows CRT can dispatch CPU-specific memory routines even when application code targets SSE2.

Compiler assembly was read from /FAs listings. A separate run samples instruction pointers only after a thread's CPU time advances. Threads are suspended briefly for context capture, then resumed before allocation or symbol lookup. Sampled runs are excluded from performance medians. Samples identify code locations; they are not retired instruction counts and have scheduling and wait-site bias. Scalar SSE or scalar AVX instructions do not process several independent mesh vertices at once.

The SSE2 probe actually executes vmovdqu and vmovntdq with YMM registers in VCRUNTIME memory routines. MSVC search helpers also execute AVX2 integer instructions such as vpmovmskb and vpmaskmovd. Thus the baseline already uses CPU-specific vector memory and search code. This does not make the application corner loop an AVX2 geometry kernel. No FMA instruction was found in the inspected normal-generation assembly.

Instruction-sampled runProcess wall sSampler CPU sIP samplesFailed suspensions
prepare48.463.8813760
annotation48.033.8313600

System-wide thread snapshots still account for most sampler CPU time. The records retain inventory and context-capture costs. The first sampler trial used much more CPU and was discarded from conclusions. Short stages have few samples; zero samples do not mean zero execution. CPU-progress filtering still permits wait-site samples because Windows thread CPU counters have coarse resolution.

Full decoded samples, source lines, module offsets, and per-function static instruction categories are in the archive. Application locations have matching PDB source lines. Runtime libraries can resolve to the nearest exported symbol, including names such as _NLG_Return2; use the module offset and decoded instruction rather than treating that export name as an exact function. AVX2 compiler code is experimental and requires a compatible CPU. The comparison compiles the six loader/preparation source units and the harness with AVX2; common core libraries remain at their baseline ISA.

In this first pass, Windows rejected the WPR CPU trace with error 0xc5585011. Hardware counters were not measured in that pass. The 12 October section adds AMD core-PMC estimates for IPC, retired instructions, demand cache fills, branch misses, DTLB misses and FP work. Physical DRAM bandwidth and exact dynamic SIMD counts remain unmeasured. QueryProcessCycleTime is an OS process counter and is not used to claim IPC or an exact CPU frequency.

Asynchronous annotation work

The current viewer prepares this cache on a separate worker after scene publication. It is not added to initial CPU preparation time. It validates geometry fingerprints, creates triangle centroid keys, sorts them, and builds a spatial tree. It shares immutable mesh geometry. In the viewer it can compete with rendering for CPU and memory bandwidth; the isolated annotation run measures the work without concurrent rendering.

Production viewer check

The unmodified production viewer imported the real file through model.add, uploaded resources, returned scene statistics and produced a screenshot. The hidden-window RPC load took 55.76 s. A verified screenshot was returned 56.68 s after the load request. This is a completed readback endpoint, not an exact first-visible-frame time. The hidden viewer's pacing, progress callbacks, GPU upload, UI work and asynchronous preparation differ from the isolated CPU probe.

The production log reports 42.01 s of CPU loading and preparation. Its field named parse_ms is 27.14 s and includes the complete CPU mesh importer, including mapping, normals and bounds. It is not the text parser interval. Upload covers 2.823 GB. Summed upload submission steps take 1.23 s, with a longest step of 122.8 ms. The remaining 13.75 s of RPC load time includes incremental upload, frame pacing, driver work and final publication. Submission time does not equal the elapsed upload interval.

The fixed-camera recording contains 160 frames over 8.06 s. Median GPU frame time is 18.74 ms; median wall frame time is 49.96 ms. The hidden viewer caps itself at 20 FPS and uses 4× MSAA at 1280×720, with an 805×687 model viewport. CPU frame timers include waits and pacing. These data do not establish maximum rendering FPS. The recording starts after screenshot capture and can overlap annotation-cache work.

NVML reports 8 GiB of GPU memory. Peak device-wide memory use is 4.83 GiB, including other applications. Device-wide GPU busy time in the fixed-camera interval has a median of 39%. NVML returns a constant 100% for its memory-utilization field on this system; those readings are not used as a bandwidth measure. GPU rendering is outside OBJ text parsing. This check does not assign GPU busy percentages to CPU loader stages.

Rendered model. Production load, preparation, upload and frame records are in the archive. Two production viewer runs are retained; their load endpoints are about 53.9 and 55.8 s.

Priorities for an optimization change

  1. Reduce bounds work. Reuse cached whole-mesh bounds when a group covers the same complete geometry. Preserve the group's bounding-box radius rule. For general groups, use independent local reductions and merge their results. This work is deterministic and does not need shared vertex insertion.
  2. Investigate the corner loop. Preserve global first-use vertex IDs and UV/normal seam behavior. Separate index resolution from attribute gathering in a research version, or partition source-position ownership and order final IDs by first corner. Measure the extra buffers and passes. The current primary shortcut already avoids most hashing.
  3. Use the AVX2 result narrowly. The compiler experiment saves 5.74 s on this CPU. Consider CPU dispatch for the measured bounds/coordinate kernels, with an SSE2 fallback. A global AVX2 build raises the minimum CPU requirement. Wide math alone does not fix mapping's dependencies.
  4. Check eager point preparation. The point hierarchy costs 5.43 s before upload even with markers off. Deferring it moves that cost to first use. Picking, marker IDs, group counts and cancellation must retain correct behavior.
  5. Reduce allocation growth. UV seams add 523,746 vertices (1.36% of render vertices), but vector growth reserves much more than the required count. Compare a better initial estimate, bounded chunks, or a two-pass count without repeating the entire expensive mapping pass.
  6. Keep parser work in proportion. Parsing is 13.3% of this CPU preparation total, and 21.3% of CPU import alone. Even removing parsing completely would improve preparation throughput by at most 1.15×. RGB values account for extra numeric conversion, but are already discarded without a colour buffer. Any faster handling must retain syntax and finite-value validation.

As a work-priority model, halving corner mapping with no added work would save about 7.55 s and improve CPU preparation throughput by 1.21×. This is an upper estimate for that change, not a measured optimization. Parallel mapping can add sorting, buffers and ordering costs that reduce the gain.

cmake --build --preset vs2026-vcpkg --config Release
ctest --preset vs2026-vcpkg -C Release
uv run experiments/obj-profile/run.py build/vs2026-vcpkg/bin/Release/woby_obj_profile_sse2.exe "D:\temp\obj_tests\20190810_BearTrap_Ground_Model.obj" --modes parser --workers 1,2,4,8,16 --rounds 3 --output build/parser-scaling.json

For the paired compiler comparison, use --modes prepare --workers 16 --rounds 3 --compare-executable build/vs2026-vcpkg/bin/Release/woby_obj_profile_avx2.exe. For read controls, use --modes read-cached,read-native --workers 1,8,16. Add --instructions to a separate run for code-location samples. Decode samples against the matching executable before rebuilding it. The run records contain executable and probe-source SHA-256 hashes. The instruction script accepts --samples and --assembly paths. AVX2 measurements need an AVX2-capable CPU with OS support.
